text:
Harry Wills (right) poses with his manager, Paddy Mullins, on September 6, 1923.

Wills will KO Homer Smith on October 11th in Long Island City, Queens, New York.

Boxing manager Paddy Mullins is not to be confused with the legendary Irish horse trainer of the same name.

From the August 15, 1925 edition of The New York Times:

Paddy Mullins, manager of Harry Wills, attached his signature yesterday to a preliminary agreement for a world's heavyweight championship match with Jack Dempsey, to be fought somewhere in the Middle West next July. Floyd Fitzsimmons, boxing promoter of Michigan City, Ind., and Benton Harbor, Mich., felt so confident that he had the match closed that he left on the 6 o'clock train last night for Chicago.

From the August 23, 1926 issue of Time magazine:

Endlessly the controversy has raged as to William Harrison Dempsey’s present boxing status. Is he on contract with Patrick Mullins, manager of black Harry Wills, to meet that fighter in Chicago? If not, is he at liberty to fight Eugene Tunney in New York in September? Last week the New York State Athletic Commission restored Dempsey to good standing. Promoter “Tex” Rickard ordered a printer to begin making tickets for the fight (top price $27.50). Patrick Mullins, meeting Fighter Dempsey, called him a liar, a cheat, offered to fight him. A humorous spectator, as he helped to pinion the spindle arms of Manager Mullins, asked loudly that Mr. Mullins be arrested on a charge of attempted suicide. Then the license committee refused Fighter Dempsey a license. Said “Tex” Rickard: “Dempsey and Tunney will fight.”

From The San Pedro News of March 25, 1932:

Paddy Mullins, Famed Boxer Manager, Dead

NEW YORK, March 25 (UP)— Paddy Mullins, shrewd, silent Irishman who rose from the welter of Bowery slums to become one of the world’s best known boxing managers, is dead.
The "silent one” who opened his 'mouth on a memorable occasion to call Jack Dempsey a liar, died yesterday of heart disease at his Brooklyn home. He was 70.
It was manager for Harry Wills, so-called "black panther,” that Mullins gained the most publicity. - In behalf of the negro heavyweight. Mullins persistently challenged the then champion. Jack Dempsey, to fight. And after Dempsey had lost his title to Gene Tunney, he shifted his barrage of challenges to the new champion.
Although Wills never was given an opportunity to meet either Dempsey or Tunney, his manager’s propaganda created the widespread impression that both were afraid of him.
Mullins once accosted Dempsey at a meeting of the, boxing commission and accused him of having run out on a bout in Chicago. Dempsey protested he was accused falsely. Whereupon Mullins shouted, “you’re a liar and you know it.” He Invited Dempsey down stairs to fight it out, but Jack smilingly declined to mix it with the grayhaired veteran.

THE BEST IS YET TO COME

The NFL Draft has twice produced a record six first-round quarterbacks—1983 and 2024. Could the Class of 2027 make it a lucky seven?

It’s a tall order, but the talent pool looks deep, and the list of quarterback-needy teams could be even deeper. Here are the top 7 candidates preparing to crash the first-round party and perhaps establish a new NCAA record:

1. Arch Manning, Texas: The famous bloodline fuels the hype, but the talent validates it. Manning possesses better raw tools than uncles Peyton and Eli and enters the season as an early favorite to go No. 1 overall. Remember, he had the top QBR of all college quarterbacks from November on out last season.

2. Dante Moore, Oregon: Some scouts believed Moore could have been the second player selected this year. Instead, he returned for another season of polish while directing one of the nation’s leading championship contenders. Moore was a stat machine before arriving in college, passing for 9,880 yards and 135 touchdowns during his high school career—nearly seven TD passes for every interception.

3. Drew Mestemaker, Oklahoma State: After leading the FBS in passing yards and touchdowns at North Texas, Mestemaker followed head coach Eric Morris to Stillwater. The tools are raw, but the ceiling is first-round high. Here's the Hollywood script: Mestemaker was a backup quarterback, punter, and safety in high school and walked on at North Texas.

4. CJ Carr, Notre Dame: Carr flourished as a redshirt freshman, firing 24 touchdown passes against only six interceptions, which tied for the most by a Notre Dame quarterback through his first 12 career starts since Terry Hanratty in 1966. Now comes the heavier lifting after the Irish lost first-round running backs Jeremiyah Love and Jadarian Price, along with third-round targets Malachi Fields and Eli Raridon. The lineage is there: His Grandfather is former Wolverines national-championship coach Lloyd Carr.

5. LaNorris Sellers, South Carolina: At 6-foot-4 and 245 pounds, Sellers looks as if he were built in a quarterback laboratory. However, after entering last season as a possible No. 1 pick, his stock slipped. This fall offers a chance to reboot the computer. Sellers has already completed his coursework and will graduate in December. His only off-field assignment this fall is an internship at a local driving range. If he straightens out his game, his draft stock could land right down the middle of the first-round fairway.

6. Trinidad Chambliss, Ole Miss: The former Division II star led the SEC with 3,937 passing yards and carried the Rebels into the CFP semifinals. Lane Kiffin may be gone, but Chambliss’ dual-threat talent remains impossible to ignore. Chambliss received no stars as a high-school recruit and became the first Ole Miss quarterback since Eli Manning in 2001 to pass for at least 250 yards in each of his first six starts.

7. Darian Mensah, Miami: Mensah led the ACC with 34 touchdown passes before transferring from Duke for a reported $6.5 million NIL package. With a stronger supporting cast in Coral Gables, he has a golden opportunity to turn that payday into a first-round ticket. Mensah once fired 211 consecutive passes without an interception, another Duke record. He led Duke to its first outright ACC championship since 1962, earning MVP honors in the game. He is the highest-paid athlete in the class of 2026.

8. Julian Sayin, Ohio State: Sayin finished fourth in the Heisman voting after tossing 32 touchdown passes and leading the nation with a sizzling 77% completion rate, the third-highest in FBS history, trailing only Bo Nix and Mac Jones, who each completed 77.4%. Now a team captain, he pilots a Buckeyes squad operating under championship-or-bust orders. Sayin's debut season brought a trophy haul: Heisman finalist, National Freshman of the Year, Big Ten Freshman of the Year, and second-team All-American.

City of Prescott Water Issues Subcommittee July, August, September 2026 Meetings Report | The Sky Isn’t Falling—But There’s Plenty to Dig Into

What is our Water Issues Subcommittee talking about and approving? The members of the subcommittee are: Mayor Cathey Rusing, and council members Lois Fruhwirth and Jim Garing. To see upcoming agendas for Water Issues subcommittee meetings, go to this City of Prescott webpage, and click on the date you want. Here you will find the agenda, meeting ”packet” and minutes if you go to a past meeting. Meeting packets include all slides shown by presenters at the meeting.

New water allocations, long-range aquifer modeling and activity at Big Chino
Just when you thought it was safe to escape Prescott’s groundwater conversations, they suck you back in. The short version? The sky isn’t falling!

The longer version is considerably more interesting—and it has uncovered enough new questions about groundwater, growth, Big Chino Water Ranch and outside conservation organizations that Prescott Pulse is launching a new Water Series.

Water Budget: What Prescott Allocated
The July 7 WIS report closed out Prescott’s January–June Water Budget. The City started the period with 25 acre-feet (AF) available for residential development and another 25 AF for non-residential development.

Residential approvals used 11.93 AF, leaving 13.07 AF.

Smaller non-residential projects used 8.39 AF, leaving 16.61 AF.

Another 14.62 AF serving 86 residential units moved forward under existing contracts or entitlements and was tracked separately from the regular Water Budget.

Deep Well Commercial Development — Jenna Lane/Hwy. 89: 27.9 AF. The City’s tracking sheet specifically says that 27.9 AF does not come out of the regular Water Budget.

The July 1–December 31 budget started the clock again with another 25 AF residential and 25 AF non-residential.

According to the September 1 WIS documents: No residential allocations had been approved as of August 20. Five smaller commercial projects had used only 2.15 AF, leaving 22.85 AF available.

Willow Creek Road and Haas Boulevard: a proposed 50-acre mixed-use development with retail, senior living, hotel, medical uses and residential development. City staff estimated total water demand at 120.29 AF per year. The property has an existing agreement for 60 AF, but City legal counsel said the proposed change in use could eliminate that entitlement. WIS tabled the application for additional work rather than recommending approval.

Dignity Health/YRMC Deep Well Ranch Campus: a phased healthcare development on approximately 16.25 acres that could eventually reach 150,000 square feet. City staff estimated total water demand at 18.02 AF per year, enough to require an appeal of the Water Budget’s 50% rule. WIS recommended the project move forward to Council.

Neither application provided in the WIS materials states a final requested AF allocation.

Long Term Water Management Plan (LTWMP): Declining Doesn’t Mean Disappearing
On August 11, City Council got its first substantial look at groundwater modeling being developed for Prescott’s Long-Term Water Management Plan.

Near the Little Chino Wellfield, monitoring shows the deeper aquifer used by City production wells declining about 0.9 feet per year. Consultants described the broader Little Chino decline as roughly one foot annually (a very small amount), with somewhat larger drawdowns nearer Prescott Valley’s wellfields.

But groundwater doesn’t behave uniformly across the basin.

Near the Airport Wellfield, deeper monitoring wells are declining while some shallow wells have actually risen, which consultants attribute to recharge at Prescott’s underground storage facility.

Now for the number that puts the Chicken Little version of Prescott’s water story into perspective.

The model estimates roughly 450 feet of saturated aquifer thickness beneath both City wellfields under baseline conditions. Over the next 50 years, preliminary modeling projects approximately:

• 80 feet of decline at the Chino Wellfield

• 40 feet of decline at the Airport Wellfield

Those numbers matter. They demand management and planning. But they do not describe an aquifer about to run dry.

And the projections aren’t fortune telling. Consultants caution that modeled water levels can differ from measured conditions by as much as 100 feet at some locations. Future studies will address the much more practical issue: how declining water levels could eventually affect the City’s ability to produce water from its wells.

The model also assumes growth. It increases pumping from existing Chino Valley and Prescott Valley municipal wells 2% annually and assumes approximately 6,900 exempt wells use half an acre-foot each per year, with that demand also growing 2% annually.

Change the assumptions and the future changes. The LTWMP will evaluate conservation, infrastructure, additional Airport wells, septic-to-sewer projects, stormwater, the City’s lakes and other options over 10-, 25- and 50-year planning horizons. The City’s stated purpose is to maintain a stable supply for current and future needs—not sound an alarm bell.

And Then There’s Big Chino
Prescott continues to identify the Big Chino Project as part of its long-term water picture. But while researching the LTWMP and September WIS meeting documents, another story emerged.

The City is working with The Nature Conservancy (TNC) on watershed-restoration projects at the City-owned Big Chino Water Ranch. The September 1 presentation discussed channel reconnection, baffles and low-tech restoration intended to change how water moves across portions of the ranch. One proposed channel-reconnection design came with an estimated price tag of more than $3.2 million, prompting TNC and City staff to consider a less expensive hybrid approach combining limited channel reconnection with baffles and other lower-tech restoration methods.

On its face, slowing erosion and keeping water on the landscape sound a lot like traditional good land stewardship.

But TNC isn’t simply an engineering contractor. It is a major environmental organization (which has 100% bought into “Climate Change” narratives) with broader policy goals. TNC Arizona says its projects contribute to organizational United Nations Agenda 2030 Goals (SDG 6.4, 6.5, 6.6) involving freshwater, lands, people and climate adaptation, while its Verde River work seeks to sustain streamflow and replenish aquifers.

That raises questions worth asking, not conclusions worth jumping to.
What exactly is TNC’s role at Prescott’s Water Ranch?

Who pays?

What does Prescott receive?

Could restoration agreements affect future use of the property?

And how do TNC’s broader goals for Big Chino and the Verde intersect with Prescott’s legal right to eventually pump and transport Big Chino groundwater?

Those questions don’t fit neatly into a WIS meeting recap. They deserve their own reporting.

A New Prescott Pulse Water Series
So we’re heading back down the water rabbit hole (you know, Whiskey’s for Drinking, Water’s for Fighting!).

Upcoming installments will dig deeper into what Prescott’s aquifer numbers really mean, what’s actually available at the Big Chino Water Ranch, the agreements governing the Water Ranch, The Nature Conservancy’s growing role in the Big Chino watershed, conservation easements and groundwater restrictions, federal and private funding, and the decades-old relationship among Prescott, Prescott Valley and SRP over the Upper Verde.

Some findings may reassure readers. Others may raise uncomfortable questions. Either way, we’ll follow the documents.

For now, Prescott’s latest groundwater modeling offers a useful starting point: our aquifers require management, but the data don’t show the sky falling.

Chicken Little can stand down. Prescott Pulse, however, is diving deeper!

The next Water Issues subcommittee meeting is scheduled for October 6, 2026.

Jeffrey Sila Ndungi’s downfall was triggered by greed, a flashy lifestyle that drew local police attention, and a critical operational mistake that allowed the US government to lure him out of his safe digital haven in Nairobi.

In, 2014, Ndungi used the stolen identity of an American citizen named Cynthia H. Short to claim a massive tax refund. The fraudulent paperwork claimed she worked for Aureus Radiology LLC in Omaha, Nebraska, earning wages that qualified her for a $76,592.86 (approx. Sh7.6 million) refund.

In the refund application, Ndungi explicitly listed a physical address, P.O. Box 925, Uhuru Gardens, Nairobi, as the mailing address. When the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) called the Nebraska company to verify Ms. Short's employment, the company confirmed they had no record of her. This flagged the check, triggering the internal  multi-year IRS sting operation. 

After flagging the suspicious $76,592.86 tax refund check filed under the name of a deceased woman (Cynthia Short), the IRS did not freeze the account or alert Ndungi.

In 2016, an undercover IRS Criminal Investigation agent established contact with Jeffrey Sila Ndungi. The agent posed as a corrupt stateside buyer looking to purchase stolen or fraudulent US Treasury checks at a discount. text:
Warren Buffett paid more than $55 million for control of a furniture company without an audit. The contract was one page.

Six years later, its 95-year-old founder walked out and opened a rival business across the street.

Her name was Rose Blumkin. She arrived in America from Russia with no formal education and learned English from her daughter. In 1937, she used $500 to open Nebraska Furniture Mart.

Her rule was simple. Sell cheap and tell the truth.

When suppliers tried to cut her off for underpricing established retailers, she found new sources elsewhere. By 1983, one Omaha location was generating more than $100 million in annual sales, exceeding the combined volume of its local competitors.

Buffett had watched that record for years. On August 30 of that year, his 53rd birthday, he made the cash offer. Mrs. B was 89.

Berkshire did not count the inventory, verify the receivables, or check the property titles. Mrs. Blumkin gave Buffett her word. He wrote the check.

The 13-minute footage attached to this post captures the acquisition as it happened. Buffett says buying a company without an audit was almost unheard of.

Mrs. B remained chairman. Her son Louie and grandsons Ron and Irv continued managing Nebraska Furniture Mart with her.

In May 1989, at 95, a management dispute with her relatives led her to leave.

Three months later, she opened Mrs. B's Warehouse directly opposite Nebraska Furniture Mart.

At the end of 1992, now 99, Mrs. B rejoined Nebraska Furniture Mart. This time, she signed a non-compete agreement.

Buffett later called his failure to obtain that protection a mistake.

Mrs. B had not broken her word. No agreement prevented her from leaving or competing.

Trust closed the first deal.

The missing clause brought Buffett back nine years later.

Watch this 13-min rare video. It's the only handshake deal Berkshire ever made at that size.

text:
Sen. John Fetterman is facing unusually fierce criticism from fellow Pennsylvania Democrats following a Wall Street Journal report questioning his engagement with some of the basic responsibilities of his office.

The backlash has moved beyond ordinary disagreements over policy, with prominent Democrats now openly pointing toward 2028 and suggesting Pennsylvania voters should replace him.

The report, based partly on internal communications and interviews with former staff members, portrayed Fetterman as frequently resistant to constituent meetings, public appearances and other traditional Senate responsibilities while devoting considerable attention to Israel and media appearances.

Fetterman and his office did not respond to requests for comment cited in the reports, the WSJ noted.

Rep. Chris Deluzio, D-Pa., responded by declaring that Fetterman was “not up for the high office he was elected to” and warning that Pennsylvania would “do something about it in 2028.”

“There is a lot I could say about this report of John Fetterman’s pathetic behavior as a senator,” Deluzio wrote, accusing him of “laziness” and “disrespect.”

Rep. Brendan Boyle, D-Pa., offered an equally harsh assessment, calling Fetterman “a disgrace” and accusing him of being too lazy to perform the job.

The Journal highlighted internal communications involving Fetterman and his staff that quickly became ammunition for his Democratic critics.

In one exchange, an aide informed Fetterman that representatives from Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia wanted to meet over concerns involving vaccines and Medicaid cuts.

Fetterman questioned the need for another meeting and reportedly responded, “I’m convinced they just want free trips to D.C.”

Another exchange involved a funeral for three Pennsylvania police officers, with an aide informing Fetterman that the service had a dress code and was expected to last approximately three hours.

“This may be a nonstarter,” Fetterman reportedly replied.

The criticism represents a striking development for a politician who entered the Senate in 2023 after campaigning as a progressive populist and longtime supporter of Sen. Bernie Sanders.

Since arriving in Washington, however, Fetterman has increasingly broken with other Democrats on several prominent issues, particularly Israel, immigration and aspects of President Donald Trump’s agenda.

Fetterman also joined Republicans during a government funding fight and has supported several Trump administration nominees.

Among them was former Oklahoma Sen. Markwayne Mullin, whom Trump nominated as secretary of Homeland Security and the Senate confirmed 54-45 in March.

Fetterman voted for Mullin’s confirmation, citing his relationship with his former Senate colleague and saying the country needed leadership at the Department of Homeland Security.

He notably voted against another Trump nominee, Dr. Mehmet Oz, his Republican opponent in Pennsylvania’s 2022 Senate election.

Fetterman has repeatedly rejected speculation that his disagreements with Democrats mean he intends to switch parties, and his overall voting record continues to include substantial alignment with his Democratic colleagues.

The anger surrounding the latest report, however, centers less on Fetterman’s ideology than allegations about his willingness to perform the everyday responsibilities expected of a senator.

That frustration has spread beyond Pennsylvania’s congressional delegation to state Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta, who also serves as a vice chair of the Democratic National Committee.

“This report is horrifying, but not new to many of us in PA,” Kenyatta wrote, accusing Fetterman of frequently being absent both as lieutenant governor and as senator.

Kenyatta also criticized Fetterman’s frequent appearances on Fox News and his positions on Israel before ending his message with an unmistakable reference to the senator’s next election.

“2028 can’t come soon enough,” he wrote.

Fetterman’s current term expires after the 2028 election, meaning Democrats unhappy with his performance would have an opportunity to challenge him in the party’s Senate primary, Fox News reported.

The Wall Street Journal also reported that potential Democratic challengers are already considering possible 2028 campaigns as Fetterman becomes increasingly isolated from parts of his party.

The article argues that economic pressure might weaken an enemy, but history suggests it may not enough by itself.  The article references the Union blockade that damaged the Confederacy during the Civil War, but victory ultimately required control of territory, the Mississippi River, and soldiers on the ground.  

What interests me most about the article is that Lincoln and the Civil War never seem to fade from our collective memory.  In troubling moments, we repeatedly look back to Lincoln and the Civil War for guidance.

In this case, I'm not sure the Civil War offers perfect guidance.  Union strategy evolved over four years of civil war.  And, of course, Iran is not the Confederacy.  The geography, military situation, political objectives, and international conditions are all very different.

text:
NEBIUS $NBIS ADDED $4.3 BILLION IN A DAY. THE BUSINESS IS UNDER TWO YEARS OLD:

Nebius Group NBIS at $226.39 Friday, +$15.76 / +7.48% - a gain that added roughly $4.3 billion to what the market says this company is worth, in one session. US markets are shut Monday, September 7 for Labor Day; the next session is Tuesday, September 8.

This week's board splits into two kinds of growth: five names below grew by charging more for about the same activity, or by getting bought outright; Nebius grew by building faster than almost anyone can verify, funded partly by money it does not yet fully hold. Both are real growth. Only one is guaranteed to look the same in a year.

The Hypergrowth Len5 is watching Nebius for the plainest reason that style exists: a business still early and fast enough to keep compounding. It rents out data centers full of the specialized chips that train and run artificial intelligence - customers pay for computing time instead of building their own hardware. The business in its current form is under two years old: it was Yandex N.V., the Dutch parent of Russia's largest search engine, until 2024, when Yandex sold its Russian search, maps and ride-hailing operations to Russian investors for $5.4 billion after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine forced a split. What relisted as Nebius was the data centers and a few software units left behind - which is why its longer growth record reads as messy rather than useful.

The current picture is not messy. Reported August 12: revenue $582.3 million, +454% year over year and +46% from the prior quarter; AI-cloud revenue alone grew 514%. Adjusted cash profit - earnings before interest, taxes and non-cash costs - swung to a positive $236 million, a 41% margin, from a loss a year ago. Customers have paid $9 billion in advance, and total commitments now top $40 billion.

The bill: $5.7 billion of building spending in that one quarter against $8 billion of cash on hand, with the full year mapped at $20 billion to $25 billion. Nebius also raised its year-end power capacity target - the electricity available to run its computers - to 5 gigawatts from 4. That gap between what it earns and what it spends to grow is the real bet in Friday's price. Next report: November 10.

MOMENTUM LEN5:
Varex Imaging, ticker VREX, at $18.51 Friday, -$0.01 / -0.05%, a cent off its 52-week high. It builds the X-ray tubes and detectors inside medical scanners and airport security machines. Momentum liked the chart: all three lookback windows agreed, at a high with an unusually calm range. The real mover landed the same day as its numbers - August 10, alongside 4% revenue growth to $211 million, Teledyne Technologies agreed to buy the company for $18.90 a share cash, a 52% premium. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: the still-undated shareholder vote - the deal isn't expected to close before early 2027, and Friday's price, thirty-nine cents under the offer, is already pricing the deal, not the chart.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
Philip Morris International at $182.53 Friday, -$3.64 / -1.96%. It sells cigarettes outside the US alongside what is meant to replace them - IQOS heated-tobacco sticks and ZYN nicotine pouches. Quality-Value wants a hard-to-copy business at a fair price, and the hard-to-copy half is settled: revenue rose 10.4% to $11.2 billion last quarter in a shrinking-smoker industry. Reported July 22: smoke-free revenue +14.2%, adjusted profit $2.20 a share, +15.2% and ahead of estimates - yet guidance stayed put, the upside redirected into a US push for ZYN. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: ZYN's own shipments, down 23.5% in the first quarter before recovering just 1.8% in the second - a third choppy quarter undercuts the story the price assumes.

DEEP-VALUE AND SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
Old Dominion Freight Line at $185.87 Friday, +$0.12 / +0.06%, about 26% under its own $252.03 high. It hauls partial truckloads for multiple shippers through a dense network of local terminals, slow and costly to permit again from scratch. Deep-Value wants a good business priced under what it looks worth after something visible went wrong - here, a freight recession: tons hauled per day fell 4.1% last quarter even as revenue rose 10.4% to $1.55 billion and EPS hit $1.68, +32.3%, tying a company record - all from charging more per shipment, not moving more freight. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: tons per day turning positive, meaning the freight recession has actually eased.

GROWTH LEN5:
Trustmark Corporation at $46.62 Friday, +$0.56 / +1.22%. The Mississippi bank takes deposits and lends across the South. Growth wants cheap growth, measured by PEG - price-to-earnings divided by expected earnings growth, where under 1 flags a bargain - and Trustmark's 0.81 comes with five straight profitable years behind it, under 12 times trailing profit. Last quarter: net income $63.5 million, EPS $1.08, deposits up 2.3%, bad loans down 47.3% - but lending stalled as $652 million of commercial real estate loans got paid off faster than new ones replaced them. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: loan growth resuming now that this quarter's payoffs are behind it.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
Nebius Group, treated above. What earns the spot beyond the headline growth rate: contracted electricity capacity, the physical limit on how much computing it can sell, was raised to 5 gigawatts for year-end 2026 from 4, with at least one more gigawatt planned every year from 2027 - a construction plan, not just a revenue projection. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: growth itself slowing as comparisons get harder. Beating a small base by 454% is a different problem than beating the much larger base it now carries forward.

INCOME LEN5:
Smithfield Foods at $21.97 Friday, -$0.06 / -0.27%, a 5.7% dividend yield. It raises hogs and turns them into fresh pork and packaged meat like bacon and hot dogs, keeping the profit at each step. Income wants a payout the business actually funds, not just a big number beside a beaten-down price, and this one is covered almost exactly twice: the $0.3125 quarterly dividend against $0.62 of adjusted profit per share last quarter. That same report trimmed full-year guidance for packaged meats and fresh pork, citing cautious consumers and higher freight, fuel and packaging costs. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: another guidance cut next quarter, meaning the caution is a trend, not one quarter's flag.

Line them up and the split holds. Five businesses here are proving they can raise prices, hold volume, or get bought outright, in unglamorous industries. The sixth is proving it can raise money and pour concrete faster than the other five combined. Both are legitimate ways to grow. Only the first kind survives a year when the money gets harder to raise.

Warren Buffett paid more than $55 million for control of a furniture company without an audit.

The contract was one page.

Six years later, its 95-year-old founder walked out and opened a rival business across the street.

Her name was Rose Blumkin.

She arrived in America from Belarus in 1917. No formal education. No English. She learned the language from her daughter.

In 1937, she borrowed $500 from her brother and opened Nebraska Furniture Mart in the basement of her husband's shop in Omaha.

Her rule was simple. Sell cheap and tell the truth.

When manufacturers refused to sell to her for underpricing established retailers, she drove to Kansas City, Chicago, and New York. Bought furniture at full retail from department stores. Brought it back to Omaha. And still sold it cheaper than anyone in town.

By 1983, one Omaha location was generating more than $100 million in annual sales.

Buffett had watched that record for years. On August 30 of that year, his 53rd birthday, he made the cash offer. Mrs. B was 89.

Mrs. B gave Buffett her word. He wrote the check.

text:
It was not true that women throughout the United States were prohibited from serving on juries until 1975.

By 1974, women were legally eligible for jury service in every state. Mississippi—the final state with an outright prohibition—allowed women to serve beginning in 1968. Alabama ended its prohibition in 1967; South Carolina had done so earlier. Equal Justice Initiative

What happened in 1975 concerned Louisiana:

Louisiana technically permitted women to serve.
But a woman could not be selected unless she had previously filed a written declaration volunteering for jury duty.
Consequently, very few women entered jury pools; one challenged pool contained no women.
On January 21, 1975, the Supreme Court ruled in Taylor v. Louisiana that this systematic exclusion violated the constitutional requirement that jury pools represent a fair cross-section of the community. Louisiana had already repealed the provision effective January 1, 1975. Supreme Court decision

Missouri also continued giving women an automatic exemption from jury service after Taylor. That system was declared unconstitutional in Duren v. Missouri in 1979.

Women were eligible to serve on juries throughout the United States by 1968, but discriminatory rules continued to keep women out of many jury pools. In 1975, the Supreme Court prohibited their systematic exclusion.

In 1974 specifically, no state appears to have prohibited all women outright. Louisiana was the clearest place where an “opt-in” requirement effectively excluded most women.

The reasoning behind the Louisiana policy.

Louisiana treated women’s jury service as optional because lawmakers assumed that many women had essential household and child-care responsibilities. Requiring women to volunteer in advance spared them from being summoned and then having to request an individual hardship exemption.

The Supreme Court acknowledged that:

Jury service might indeed create hardship for many women.
Determining individually who qualified for an exemption could be administratively burdensome.
States could still grant reasonable exemptions for child care or genuine hardship.

However, the Court ruled that Louisiana could not presume that every woman needed an exemption based solely on sex. The practical result was nearly all-male jury pools: although women represented 53% of eligible citizens in the district examined, only 12 of 1,800 people summoned during the relevant period were women. Taylor v. Louisiana

The rule offered women a choice and was presented as protecting them from a burden—not as an outright declaration that women were incapable of jury service. The Court objected because that blanket protection effectively excluded women as a class, instead of providing individual hardship exemptions to women or men who actually needed them.

Here is a common soldier who could not read or write, who twice charged into a storm of enemy fire to save a flag, and who turned down the chance to become an officer because he thought himself too lowly for the honor. His name was Sergeant William Jasper, and he understood something about courage and about pride that most people never learn.

Jasper's first great moment came on June 28, 1776, at a half-finished little fort on Sullivan's Island guarding Charleston harbor. A powerful British fleet sailed in to blast the place to rubble and open the door to the South. But the fort's walls were built of soft, spongy palmetto logs, and instead of shattering, they simply swallowed the British cannonballs. Hour after hour the fort held, and its defenders poured fire back into the ships.

Then, in the middle of that bombardment, a British shot cut down the fort's flagstaff, and the blue flag tumbled down outside the walls, into the open, into the very teeth of the enemy guns. To the men watching from the British ships, it looked like surrender. To the Americans, it was a gut punch at the worst moment.

Sergeant Jasper would not have it. He climbed over the wall of the fort, dropped down on the outside, completely exposed, and walked out into the fire to get the flag. Cannonballs and grapeshot tore the air around him. He picked up the fallen colors, carried them back, fastened them to a sponge staff, a cannon-cleaning rod, and raised them again on the ramparts for everyone on both sides to see. The fort had not surrendered. The flag was flying. His comrades roared, and they fought on to a stunning victory that saved Charleston for years.

Jasper became a hero overnight. The governor of South Carolina was so moved that he took his own sword from his belt and presented it to the sergeant, and offered him a battlefield commission, the chance to become an officer, a gentleman, to rise far above his station. And Jasper turned it down. He said, in effect, that he was not fit to keep officers' company, that he was only a sergeant. He did not have the education, and he would not pretend to a rank he felt he had not earned in that way. He would rather stay a sergeant among the men he knew than be an officer he did not feel he deserved to be. There is a strange, humble greatness in that.

He went back to the war and became famous as a scout and a raider, pulling off daring exploits behind enemy lines, including a legendary rescue of American prisoners. But he could not stay away from the colors. In October 1779, at the bloody, failed allied assault on British-held Savannah, the fighting collapsed into a slaughter at the enemy walls. When the man carrying his regiment's flag was cut down, Jasper did the only thing his whole life had trained him to do. He seized the falling colors and tried to plant them on the British works, in the worst of the fire, one more time.

This time it killed him. He was shot down carrying the flag and mortally wounded. His comrades managed to drag him from the field, but there was no saving him, and he died a few hours later. He had given his life exactly as he had risked it three years earlier, refusing to let the flag touch the ground.

America did not forget him, even if most Americans today have. Counties in a dozen states bear the name Jasper. A monument to him still stands in a square in Savannah, near where he fell. Remember Sergeant William Jasper, the illiterate soldier who twice ran into death for a banner, who told a governor he was only a sergeant, and who proved that the truest kind of honor has nothing to do with rank.

In June 2002, 15‑year‑old Kara Robinson was watering plants outside a friend’s home in South Carolina when a man approached her with a gun and forced her into his car. He took her to his apartment, where she was held for 18 hours.
Despite the fear and isolation, Kara stayed remarkably calm. She spoke to him gently, answered his questions, and made herself seem non‑threatening, all while quietly studying everything around her. She memorized names on refrigerator magnets, noticed paperwork on counters, and took in details about the apartment layout. She even offered to clean, using the opportunity to move around and gather more clues.
When her captor finally fell asleep, Kara saw her chance. She slipped out of the restraints, eased out the door, and ran to safety. Within hours, she was giving police a detailed description of the man, his home, and the evidence inside.
Her information led investigators straight to the suspect, who was later identified as a serial killer responsible for multiple murders across several states. Kara’s courage and presence of mind not only saved her own life, but helped end a deadly pattern of violence.

$PARR Par Pacific: Evaluating Mid-Cycle Value and Strategic Growth Beyond 2026. Investment Thesis. New: 9/5/26.

Par Pacific operates in a refining geography that provides structural margin advantages unavailable to mainland commodity refiners — Hawaii's island isolation creates a captive regional market where logistics barriers and limited competition support crack spreads that normalize above continental U.S. levels regardless of the broader refining cycle. That geographic moat is the foundational competitive advantage that distinguishes Par Pacific from peers and justifies a structural premium over the commodity refining multiple.

The Billings acquisition extended the geographic footprint and added a landlocked refinery whose margin profile is driven by different regional dynamics than Hawaii — specifically, crude sourcing advantages from Bakken and Canadian production and regional product market access that creates localized supply-demand economics. The integration of that asset alongside the Hawaii operations creates a more diversified earnings base, though it also introduces a refinery whose competitive position is more contested than the island market that defines Par Pacific's historical differentiation.

Balance sheet de-risking is the financial improvement that converts the operational quality into investable form. A leveraged refining company in a cyclical industry carries existential risk through the trough that a clean balance sheet eliminates, and the debt reduction work that has been accomplished changes the character of the equity from a highly levered cyclical bet to a fundamentally sound business with refining exposure. That distinction matters for the investor base the company can attract and the valuation multiple it can sustain.

Small refinery exemptions are the regulatory variable that carries the same uncertainty for Par Pacific as for other SRE-dependent refiners. The Hawaii refinery's size relative to RFS thresholds creates exemption eligibility that is financially material when granted and a compliance cost burden when denied — and the regulatory trajectory on SRE policy is not reliably foreseeable across EPA administration changes. Building forward earnings assumptions on continued SRE contribution requires a regulatory confidence that the history of that program doesn't support.

The Hawaii Renewables project is the long-duration strategic optionality that extends the investment narrative beyond the conventional refining cycle. Sustainable aviation fuel production at the Hawaii facility addresses a specific and growing demand category — Hawaiian airlines and military aviation both have SAF procurement motivations that mainland refiners don't access as directly — but the project economics depend on regulatory support structures and feedstock availability that are still being validated.

The core investment question is whether the current stock price fully reflects the operational improvements and geographic advantages, or whether the valuation still offers upside to a normalized earnings power that is genuinely above historical averages. Capital allocation discipline — how management deploys the free cash flow that peak-cycle margins are generating — is the variable most within management's control that will determine whether the current earnings strength compounds into durable value creation or is distributed and replaced by a normalized earnings base at a lower multiple.

Don’t wait for more poles to close the holes.
By then the Fourth is already gone.

Missing children and stolen cars matter. Nobody serious is cheering for the next abduction.

The fight is not “cops vs chaos.” It is this product: cameras on the road that photograph every passing car — plate, time, place, color, stickers — and store that so police can search it later and share it. You were not a suspect when the pole clicked. You were driving.

There’s no way to rule innocent men — until every car has a trail. Then you don’t invent the person. You search for him.

Flock advocates say it is just a public plate. A cop on the corner could write the same number down. That is one look. This is a file that lasts and spreads. Police already look up who owns a plate. The camera hands them the number. The vehicle registration file hands them the name. The state’s license photo — the clear picture REAL ID made every state keep — sits in another drawer. The same government agency can open both. Two files on paper becomes one person in practice.

Flock advocates point to court cases about one town’s cameras with gaps in coverage and say the Fourth Amendment is settled. Those cases did not bless a growing shared net, or a search weeks later, or the owner lookup. A small ruling is not a big permission slip.

Flock advocates say the tool saves lives, so you wanting to impose limits means you want the grave. That is a false choice. You can want the child found and still refuse a default file on everybody. The third path is a tighter tool: short storage of all data, no extra traffic product the city never bought, no hundred searches on a man who legally filmed a cop.

Flock advocates say the fences are easy. Wisconsin deputies ran this system more than a hundred times on a Navy veteran after he recorded a stop. Sheboygan was offered years of speed and travel data it says it never approved. A log after the fact is not a lock on the door. If the tool is that handy, officials will go around the fence.

Now add software that can comb those unlocked files all at once — every plate, every time, every owner record the agency can already open — and the person at the login does not need a hunch. They need a purpose. If that purpose is control, not a single crime, the machine will serve it. Flock advocates still talk like a deputy is typing one plate for one case. A system that can sweep the linked drawers is not that deputy. It is a staff that never sleeps.

The American experiment assumed the government would have to pick a target before it got the story of your week. This stack works the other way: story first, target when needed. That is not a better flashlight. That is the end of living as someone the state has not already filed.

The Fourth Amendment is supposed to stop a bad search habit before it becomes furniture. Waiting until the holes in the map fill with more poles means you act when the tool is too useful to unwind. That is not caution. That is delay.

Do not build a memory of the innocent because the first ad was a victim. Do not pretend the drawers stay apart when the same hands hold both keys. Do not hand those hands a searcher that never gets bored. Do not wait for the holes to close.

Don’t wait for more poles to close the holes.
By then the Fourth is already gone.

In 1958, a computer learned to distinguish punch cards marked on the left from cards marked on the right. After roughly 50 training attempts, it could classify them without error.

The next morning, The New York Times reported that the U.S. Navy expected the eventual machine to "walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence."

Eleven years later, neural networks were widely being treated as a dead end.

Frank Rosenblatt’s perceptron had been misunderstood in both directions.

Rosenblatt was a 29-year-old psychologist at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory. Computing had entered his work through an unusual route => as a graduate student studying personality, he built a machine called EPAC to process psychological test data and nicknamed it the "Idiot Brain."

His larger interest was biological. How could a brain recognize something it had never seen in exactly that form before? How could experience change the way it responded next time?

Earlier researchers had supplied parts of the answer. Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts had described simplified neurons as threshold logic units. Donald Hebb had proposed that learning involved changes in the strength of connections between neurons. Rosenblatt combined this lineage with an error-correction procedure and built a trainable system for recognizing patterns.

The perceptron received an input, combined signals through weighted connections and produced a response. During training, a correct response left the relevant weights alone; an error caused them to be adjusted. For any binary classification problem that could be separated by a linear boundary, the learning procedure was guaranteed to find such a boundary after a finite number of corrections.

The 1958 demonstration took place in software on an IBM 704. The purpose-built Mark I Perceptron followed and was publicly demonstrated in 1960.

Its visual input came from a camera containing a 20×20 grid of photocells. The 400 sensory units connected to 512 association units, which fed eight binary response units. Each sensory unit could connect to as many as 40 association units, with the wiring commonly chosen from tables of random numbers.

The trainable connections were controlled by motor-driven potentiometers. Updating a weight meant physically rotating an electrical component inside the machine.

This was the part obscured by all the talk of electronic brains. Rosenblatt had demonstrated a different way of programming. Instead of specifying the complete recognition rule, the designer supplied examples and a procedure for learning from errors. The resulting behaviour was stored across the machine’s adjustable connections.

The distinction between training and programming is ordinary to us now. It was not ordinary in 1958.

The perceptron’s limitations were real. The basic classifier learned only a linear decision boundary. AND and OR could be represented this way, but XOR could not => its positive examples lie on diagonally opposite corners, so no single straight line can separate them from the negative examples.

In 1969, Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert published Perceptrons. They rigorously analysed restricted perceptron architectures and showed serious limitations on problems such as parity and determining whether regions in an image were connected. They also doubted that adding trainable layers would provide a practical escape.

The book arrived after enthusiasm had already begun to fade. Early results had not justified the publicity, computers were severely constrained, effective training of multiple adaptive layers remained unresolved, and funding priorities were changing. Its publication helped solidify the belief that neural networks offered little room for progress, but it did not mathematically prove that every neural-network architecture was useless.

Rosenblatt knew that the simple perceptron was inadequate for many problems. His 1962 book examined multilayer and cross-coupled systems while openly listing the difficulties that still had to be solved. His disagreement with Minsky, a former schoolmate from the Bronx High School of Science, was not over whether the early machines were limited. It was over whether those limits justified abandoning the approach.

Rosenblatt died in a sailing accident in Chesapeake Bay on July 11, 1971, his 43rd birthday. He did not live through the revival of neural-network research in the 1980s.

Earlier formulations of backpropagation already existed, but the influential 1986 work of David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams demonstrated how it could train hidden layers to develop useful internal representations. Subsequent advances in architectures, data and computing power pushed neural networks far beyond anything the Mark I could do.

Modern Transformers bear little architectural resemblance to Rosenblatt’s machine. They use attention, differentiable nonlinearities and gradient-based optimization across enormous parameter spaces. The shared principle is more fundamental: useful behaviour can be learned by adjusting a network’s internal connections in response to data.

Once the 1958 hype and the later dismissal are removed, Rosenblatt’s achievement needs little embellishment. He built an early working learning system and helped turn adaptation from examples into an engineering discipline.

Modern AI grew from taking that possibility seriously.

That is the part that bothers me. Because it is easy to put a camera in front of a tragedy and tell the public who the heroes are. It is easy to show a dead baby, a dumpster, police tape, grieving relatives and a reporter standing outside the scene. It is easy to tell people that an organization is helping children and families. Olive Crest publicly describes its mission as strengthening, equipping and restoring children and families in crisis, and its Nevada operation openly describes programs involving foster families, family preservation, mental health and other services. Fine. Those services can be evaluated on their actual performance. But Project Stone is not interested in the commercial. Project Stone is interested in the paper trail.

So give me the call. Give me the timestamp. Give me the incident number. Give me the dispatch. Give me the referral. Give me the intake record. Give me the policy that authorized the referral. Give me the contract governing the service. Give me the funding source. Give me the database entry. Give me the access log. Give me the retention policy. Give me the records-request response. Give me the explanation for every redaction. Give me the explanation for every withheld record. If the system worked, then show how it worked. If the system failed, show where it failed. If somebody made a mistake, identify the mistake. If somebody violated a policy, identify the policy. If somebody committed a crime, then investigate the crime. But don’t expect the public to accept a television narrative as a substitute for an audit trail.

And now let’s turn that demand into an actual records investigation, because this is where Project Stone stops being just a monologue and becomes a fucking records trail. First, lock down the exact date range. Don’t send somebody a request saying “give me everything about Olive Crest.” Make it specific: identify the incident date, the approximate time, the location, the agency, the program, the telephone number, the case number if known and the people or departments believed to have handled the matter. Clark County itself advises requesters to be as specific as possible, provide a date range and identify the departments or employees who may have been involved.

Second, make the 911 request separately from the child-welfare request. Ask the appropriate emergency-services custodian for the call-for-service record, CAD event, incident number, dispatch timeline, disposition, audio if releasable, and any releasable associated records for the specific date and time. Don’t mix ten different agencies into one request and then wonder why nobody knows who owns the record. Identify the actual custodian. Clark County specifically notes that it is not the custodian of police, detention or court records and directs requesters to the appropriate law-enforcement agency for those records.

Third, make a separate request for 311 or other non-emergency county records if that system is involved. Ask for the call number, date and time, originating department, disposition, referral destination, associated service request and any releasable metadata. The point is not to demand somebody else’s private information. The point is to establish whether a particular call existed, where it went and what governmental system received it.

Fourth, make a separate request to Clark County Department of Family Services. And this is where the law matters. Clark County currently states that its CPS records and agency files are confidential and cites NRS 432B.280 and NRS 127.200. DFS also explains that certain people, including a child, parent or guardian, a subject of a report, their attorney, or a person with a court order, may have access under NRS 432B.290. For eligible requesters, DFS offers a case-closure-summary request and a general-records request, and it warns that records may be redacted and that submitting a request does not guarantee access to the entire file.

There is a form of property ownership where you can never be taxed out of your own home.

It's called allodial title.

Total ownership. No landlord. Not even the government.

Compare that to what you have right now.

Fee simple title, the standard in America, means you're always a renter with extra steps.

Miss enough property tax payments on a house you paid off 20 years ago and the county takes it. Doesn't matter if your mortgage has been gone for decades.

You never actually stop paying rent. You just pay it to a different landlord.

Here's the part that should make you angry.

Nevada actually built a program for this in 1997.

Homeowners could pay a lump sum covering their future property taxes and receive a certificate of allodial title. No more annual tax bill. Ever.

For almost a decade, real Americans held title to their homes the way our ancestors once did before feudal systems bled into modern property law.

Then in 2005, Nevada shut it down.

Officially they called it "actuarially unsound."

Unofficially, imagine the tax revenue a state loses when homeowners stop paying forever instead of paying annually. Now imagine every state watching what Nevada did.

That program never had a chance of spreading. It threatened the entire business model of property taxation.

No state has offered it since. None currently do.

But the fact that it existed even once should make you ask a bigger question.

What would it take to bring it back?

Because if true ownership was possible for a few years in Nevada, it's possible again.

From British Vintage boxing on perhaps the greatest amateur boxer of all-time, Teofilo Stevenson of Cuba:

'What are eight million dollars compared to the love of eight million Cubans.’
- Teofilo  Stevenson
The above quote was in response to a very lucrative offer, to turn professional after Stevenson’s second consecutive Olympic heavyweight gold medal, at the 1976 Games. The offer was actually nearer $5 million dollars to fight nonother than Muhammad Ali. In essence, The Greatest fighting the greatest.
Despite the best efforts from the likes of Bob Arum and Don King, it was a fight which unfortunately never materialised and one which many tipped Stevenson to win. A similar offer was made a few years later to Stevenson’s successor, Félix Savón, to fight Mike Tyson and again, the offer was turned down, despite a ludicrous amount of money being offered and Savón being the favourite. So why exactly did possibly Cuba’s most famous athletes of all time turn down such life changing sums of cash? The answer is, morals and integrity……with a little bit of influencing. Also, the media and politicians decided to stick their oar in and make it a battle between Cuban Communism versus American Democracy, which certainly didn’t help to bring the fight to fruition.
It's a debate which will continue for years. Who would win? Stevenson had all the tools and power to dismantle Ali, yet, he had been primed his whole life for three round contests, under different rules. Ali on the other hand was himself an Olympic gold medallist and had been in with some of the hardest punchers in history in the pro ranks. Who would have won? We’ll never know.
Professional boxing was banned in Cuba from 1962, due to their then leader, Fidel Castro regarding the sport as corrupt and consequently convincing his fellow Cubans to compete for the glory of representing their country instead of their bank balance. As a result, many great Cuban boxers never got to test their full potential under professional rules and many others left their home country, changed nationalities and fought under the banner of other countries. 
Back to Teófilo. Another reason he declined the offer to fight Ali in 1976, is because his work in the amateur ring was far from over and he would go on to raise the bar to unparalleled heights.
Teófilo Stevenson Lawrence was Cuban born, but the exact whereabouts of his birth has never fully been confirmed. Puerto Padre is the most common answer, however, Las Tunas has also been in the mix, as has Jamaica. All we do know is that he was born on 29 March 1952.
Teófilo ’s mother, Dolores was first generation Cuban, from St Kitts heritage, whereas his father, Teófilo Stevenson Patterson, an immigrant from Saint Vincent, worked the docks and took on a number of jobs to pay the bills, including teaching English.
Stevenson Sr was a large frame of a man and had a passion for training and sparring in boxing gyms. Despite having a rumoured 10 fights as an amateur, his dislike of the payment for boxers made him give up and concentrate on gaining a trade.
However, it was Sr’s involvement in the square ring that inspired young Stevenson to lace up the gloves at nine years of age. Under the tutelage of former light heavyweight national champion, John Herrera, Stevenson started to rack up the silverware and by 1968 won gold at the Cuba Junior Championships, at light middleweight.
A knockout victory over Nancio Carrillo gained the attention of the onlookers, due to Carillo having represented Cuba at the 1968 Olympics in Mexico City. It was at this point Cuba hired in some help from the East.
Stevenson’s learning curve went vertical when he started training in Havana with the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) coach, Andrei Chervonenko, who had set up a boxing school in the country’s capital. Up to this point, Stevenson’s style was based more under the fundamentals of professional boxing, whereas Chervonenko showed him how to win fights under the amateur scoring system, through his vast experience of success with some of the best Eastern European fighters at the time.
By the age of 17, Stevenson was now boxing in the senior ranks, albeit, the vastly talented Cuban started off with two points losses against Adolfo Galvez (1986) and Gabriel Garcia (1969), in the Playa Giron - Cuban National Championships.
However, in 1970, Stevenson beat Earl McClear to win the Central American and Caribbean Championships, followed by a trip to Bulgaria, where he won three fights in six days to win the Friendship Tournament Heavyweight crown.  
In 1971, Stevenson reached the finals of the Pan American Games in Colombia, falling short against the highly talented American, Duane Bobick (the same man who would deny Larry Holmes passage to the 1972 USA Olympic Team). Stevenson did however pick up the bronze medal and the same year travelled to Germany to win the TSC tournament and also won the Playa Giron - Cuban National Championships once again.
One year later and Stevenson locked horns with Bobick again, in what was simply an outstanding fight. In 12 months, Stevenson was simply a different beast. Physically, mentally and technically, he was displaying traits of a legend in the making. On this occasion, they were paired at the 1972 Olympic Games at Munich in the quarter finals.
As the fight moved into the third and decisive final round, Stevenson floored the defiantly good, Bobick three times and in doing so progressed to the semifinals, to face German, Peter Hussing.
After smashing the German in the second round, (who claimed to have never been hit so hard before) Stevenson went on to pick up gold and consequently become the Olympic heavyweight champion, after Romanian, Ion Alexe was unable to make the final due to a broken hand. For the small number of naysayers who claimed Stevenson was gifted his prize, he would go on to prove that he was indeed, no fluke. In fact, the 1972 Olympics was to mark an unprecedented run of amateur brilliance beyond the next decade.
Stevenson despatches Peter Hussing in the semi-finals 1972 Olympic Games
In addition to his coveted Olympic gold, in the very same year, Stevenson also went on to receive the Val Barker Trophy and the Merited Master of Sport of the USSR, which is an honour rarely awarded to non-Russian nationals.
Two years later, Cuba awarded Stevenson two large houses for his continued successes in the ring, which came under attack from the AIBA president, Anwar Choudry, claiming that this practice did not run along the guidelines of the amateur system. The Cuban officials responded by saying that’s how they rewarded their athletes. End of story.
Stevenson went on to win the World Championships in 1974 in front of adorning fans in Havana, Cuba, followed by Gold at the Pan American Games in 1975.  Between 1973 – 1976, Stevenson’s only losses came at the hands of Russian, Igor Yvsotsky, which included his only ever knockout loss. Incredibly, despite 161 victories as an amateur, Yvsotsky would never compete at the Olympics.
In the summer of 1976, Stevenson wowed fans in Montreal, Canada, with a string of glowing performances, stopping the big Fin, Pekka Ruokola and future professional world heavyweight champion, John Tate in the semifinal. Former world heavyweight champion, George Foreman was commentating ringside and he was asked if he believed Stevenson had what it took to make the transition to the pro ranks. Foreman responded, ‘I haven’t seen that much class and skill in amateur or professional boxing! In my opinion, Stevenson would undoubtedly become the world heavyweight boxing champion, because he has the skill and qualifications.’
Funnily enough, comparisons of Stevenson were often made with both Foreman and Ali, in terms of having the speed, footwork and agility of Ali, whilst possessing similar power to Foreman. Standing at 6ft 4 inches, with an abundance of talent, in boxing terms, he was the complete nightmare package to meet in the ring.
After dispatching Tate, Stevenson forced Romanian, Mircea Simonto to retire in the third round of the final. He was now a double gold medal Olympian. Over 30 years later, Stevenson told Associated Press, ‘The Olympic Games in Munich and Montreal are the fondest memories I have from my life, the best stage of my career.’
Four years later, USA boycotted the Olympics in Moscow and although his route to gold was not easy, but let’s say it was ‘easier.’ Stevenson won his first two fights by stoppage, beating Hungarian Istvan Levai in the semifinal, then winning gold by beating Piotr Zaev of the Soviet Union. Although the boycotting is something which worked in Stevenson’s favour on this occasion, it turned out to be his arch enemy for the next two Olympic Games.
In 1982, Stevenson lost to Italian, Francesco Damiani at the World Championships, which scuppered his consecutive trilogy run of golds at this tournament. The Italian went on to claim silver and then two years later also gained silver on the Olympic podium in Los Angeles, at the 1984 summer Olympiad. Damiani turned professional in January 1985 and went on to become European and WBO world heavyweight champion, with a very respectable pro record of 30-2, with the two losses coming at the hands of Ray Mercer and Oliver McCall. The loss against Damiani denied Stevenson the possibility of four golds on the bounce in the World Championships.
Over the next four years, Stevenson continued to create a blaze of success, gaining gold at the Friendship Games in 1984 and a further third gold at the World Championships in 1986 in Reno, Nevada. Sadly, politics has a way of affecting the trajectory of success for so many athletes and the 1984 Olympics was no different for Stevenson, as Cuba boycotted the games. Tyrell Biggs, who Stevenson had defeated shortly before, in a Cuba versus USA tournament, went on to win the Olympic super heavyweight gold medal, which was the first time this weight class had been introduced. Once again, Stevenson was denied the chance to gain four gold medals in four consecutive major tournaments. In fact, Stevenson may well have had a chance of gaining five gold medals, had Cuba also not boycotted the 1988 Olympics in Seoul.  The boycott was the straw breaking the camel’s back for Stevenson and he retired shortly after Cuba’s withdrawal in 1988.
Although denied the chance to expand his collection of Olympic medals, in 1987, Stevenson was awarded the highly prestigious Olympic Order, which is the most distinguished award for any athlete to be awarded by the International Olympic Committee, for their contribution to sport.
Stevenson retired with a sensational amateur boxing record of 302 wins, 22 losses and eight draws, although folklore has Stevenson fighting in as many as 600 amateur contests. However, it’s not just the wins, it’s the calibre of the fights he was in, the opposition he defeated and the way he did it.
Hungarian László Papp was the first boxer to win three consecutive gold medals in the Olympics, however, Stevenson, the second to reach such fistic heights, made history by being the first to win three consecutive golds in the heavyweight ranks. Add fellow Cuban, Félix Savón into the group and the trio are the only triple consecutive Olympic boxing gold medallists in boxing history.
Stevenson went on to live in Havana, became part of the coaching detail within the national squad and held the coveted position of vice president of Cuba’s Boxing Federation. Sadly, he  died from complications relating to heart disease on 11 June 2012, in Havana Cuba. He was only 60 years old and was survived by his two children.
With what he achieved in the ring from 1966 - 1986, a lifespan of perhaps 600 years would have been more fitting for a character of such legendary status. Is Teófilo Stevenson Lawrence the most famous boxer you may never heard of, who never fought for money? Perhaps…. But now you do know him and can spread the word.
Fidel Castro commented on the news of Stevenson’s death: ‘Teófilo  Stevenson deserves the recognition of the Cuban people for his athletic success derived from his discipline, his dedication to the sport, his courage... We believe that he set a very valuable example... This young man, the humble son of a humble family... said he would not exchange his people for all the dollars in the world.’

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On the morning of September 6, 1863, while a Union army marched on Little Rock, two Confederate generals met at fifteen paces on a plantation north of the Arkansas River and tried to kill each other. The war they were supposed to be fighting waited in the next county. Honor would not.

John S. Marmaduke was West Point steel: Missouri cavalryman, impatient, certain of his own nerve, and unwilling to serve under a man he no longer trusted. Lucius M. Walker was Tennessee-born, a planter, nephew of President Polk, ranking officer over the same cavalry, and just as certain that his name had been stained. The wound between them was not a single insult. It was a chain of slights that began at Helena on the Fourth of July, tightened at Brownsville on the twenty-fifth of August, and snapped after Bayou Meto, when Marmaduke sent for Walker on the field and Walker would not come. Marmaduke decided he would no longer take orders from him. Walker demanded to know whether he had been called a coward. Marmaduke answered like a man who knows the old code by heart: he had not used the word, but the conduct was enough. He would not serve.

The notes passed through friends. Colonel Robert Crockett—grandson of Davy Crockett—and Captain John C. Moore did what seconds so often do: they sharpened the quarrel instead of cooling it. A challenge was issued. It was accepted. Major General Sterling Price, who needed both men alive, ordered them confined to quarters. Walker never received the order. Marmaduke ignored it. At dawn they stood on Godfrey LeFevre’s ground, Colt Navy revolvers loaded in every chamber, fifteen paces of damp Arkansas earth between them.

They fired. Both missed. Marmaduke recocked and fired again. The ball struck Walker in the side, tore through kidney and spine, and dropped him paralyzed. Then came the gesture that reveals the whole age: the man who had just shot him ran forward, offered his own ambulance, and heard Walker forgive him before the sacrament. That same day Walker learned a son had been born. He died the next afternoon in Little Rock.

Price arrested Marmaduke for murder. Then he released him, because Frederick Steele’s columns were already at the door and a cavalry division could not change commanders in the face of the enemy. Four days later the capital fell. The duel had decided nothing the Union could not have decided for them.

Watch the pattern. Two men bound to one flag spent their last free hours settling a private ledger of pride while the larger war moved on. Courage without mastery of the self becomes theater. Honor without proportion becomes a luxury an army cannot afford. The river kept flowing. The city did not hold. The names remain because men would rather die right than live useful.

Morning After /12
The Grand Cattleier Homestead was a farmhouse in name only. Each of Pa's three daughters — the trench-coated brunette being the youngest — kept her own alabaster dome behind a pillared façade, the entire estate elaborately protected against attempts at reconnoitre.

The night before was still a blur of contrasting impressions after Iaanda had accepted the auburn-haired woman's offer of overnight hospitality: 

opulent architecture ringed by gene-modded cacti stretching to the horizon of a reclaimed dust-plain, now painstakingly watered by gangs of indentured workers who toil until the baking sun slides behind the distant hills, massaging the crops' thorns by hand to gather drops of the hallucinogenic sap that dulls the minds of the idle wealthy across the Sector.

Dinner was resplendent, served by a dozen maskless slave-servants with dead stares, hurrying to flute music from a trio of eunuchs in black togas, who seemed to be playing for their lives. 

The Grand Cattleier was gracious and witty — though Iaanda struggled to hold her backpacking-tourist cover story together under the thrust of his deft questions.

“I find it a matter of the most wonderful exoticism that an ingenuous, off-world young woman of elevated station should deem our planet free of hazard, and so journey upon it unaccompanied,” he said, eyes emotionless.

…***…
After the digestifs, she excused herself, and the brunette — den-Maanka, now in a low-cut inky dress, her ivory mask set daringly at an angle — offered to show her to her quarters, taking her elbow. 

They walked slowly through a maze of island gardens planted with scented shrubs imported from a hundred worlds at incalculable cost, the fine mist of the sprinklers moistening both young women's faces as they talked of Galactic fashion and celebrities, and den-Maanka's dreams of escaping.

Only when the doors slid shut did Iaanda realise she stood in her host's private rooms. den-Maanka let the dress slip from her shoulders and removed her mask. 

Iaanda nodded with a grin.

…***…
She sits in den-Maanka's western atrium, enjoying her morning tea and waiting for her bed-companion to join her, a part of her chiding herself for being sidetracked from finding Sorkaii — when an armoured flier banks in at high speed and the sirens begin to wail. 

A wet-haired den-Maanka arrives breathless, one hand clutching a towel at her waist. Iaanda leaps up and tackles her lover to the floor, too late.

One of the bullets meant for her has passed through den-Maanka's forehead, and she will never whisper again in the liberating darkness how she wants to be travelling on a spaceship with somebody who cares about her. Red spreads across the azure tiles and the discarded towel.

Time to sprint.

I was going through some of my things and found this that I wrote on March 7, 2024. This photo was taken that same day with Zurita, one of our rescue dogs at the time. She has since been adopted, but I read these words again tonight and wanted to share them because, more than two years later, every word is still true.

“One of the most profound feelings on this plane is knowing an animal trusts you — and trusts you with its life. When you look into its eyes, you can feel with every fiber of your being the depth to which it trusts you.

To bring an animal into your life that has known suffering — true suffering — and to gain its trust is otherworldly. To take the time and practice the patience needed to heal its wounds, not just physically, but emotionally, mentally, and yes, even spiritually, is a gift.

To gain the full trust of an animal is a privilege.

The love that exists at LHRR is, in my opinion, unmatched. Every animal saved is a part of us. They each steal a piece of our hearts, and we carry them with us for the rest of our days. We work tirelessly to gain their trust and to be worthy of their transcending, unconditional love.

If you look into the eyes of an animal, it will tell you everything you need to know. You will learn its past, its fears, its insecurities, what it needs, and what makes it happy. They will bare their souls to you if you take the time to listen.

Animals are magnificent creatures, capable of holding a capacity for love that humans cannot even imagine. The way in which they trust and give themselves over to you fully is a bridge humans don’t have the capability of crossing.

As a rescuer, the best compliment I ever receive is, “I know how much you love your animals. I can feel the love between you and all of them, each and every one.”

LHRR is special in so many ways. We rescue dogs from shelters facing euthanasia. We rescue strays and medical cases. We have rescued from dog-fighting situations. We take behavioral dogs that no one else will. We offer sanctuary to those who are unadoptable. We provide rehabilitation and training. We help other rescues when they need it. We always stand behind our dogs. We have maintained a 100% save rate, and our family has expanded far beyond dogs.

But what I am most proud of — and what I believe makes us truly special — is the unbreakable bond we form with our rescues.

They truly are family. They are a part of us.

The love we share is sincere, authentic, genuine, and very real.” 

And that part has never changed.

A lot has changed since I wrote this in 2024.

We didn’t make it to Oregon. Instead, we purchased 20 acres in Texas and continued building a home and sanctuary for the animals who depend on us.

Some of the dogs I was loving when I wrote these words have since crossed the Rainbow Bridge. Their absence is felt every single day, and they will always be part of this rescue and part of me.

And since then, new dogs have come through our gates and made LHRR their home. More lives have found safety here. More animals have learned that they are loved, protected, and finally home.

The mission is still the same.

Love them. Protect them. Give them the time they need. And never give up on them.

But building and maintaining this place takes an incredible amount of money. We still have so much we need to build and improve here, while also covering food, veterinary care, utilities, housing, supplies, and the everyday bills that keep this sanctuary running.

Right now, during our birthday fundraiser, we desperately need your help.

We have a $2,500 match through the end of the day September 8th, and we still need approximately $2,200 to reach the full match.

If you are able to donate, now is such an important time. Every donation helps us keep building this place, pay our bills, buy food and treats, cover veterinary care, and continue giving every animal here the promise we made when they came through our gates:

You are safe now.
You are loved.
